subject: chemistry
topicDisplay: Reactivity 3.3 & 3.4 — electron sharing and electron-pair sharing
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {subject} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then mark my answer the way an IB examiner would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} {subject} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

learningObjectives.title: What a radical is and how to show one
Homolytic fission and the initiation step
Propagation, termination and the product mixture

options: A molecular entity that has an unpaired electron
A molecular entity that carries an electric charge
A group of atoms that stays together in reactions
A molecular entity with an incomplete octet
optionWhy: This is the definition: a radical has an unpaired electron, as in •CH₃ and Cl•. The unpaired electron is what makes radicals highly reactive.

You chose the definition of an ion. Radicals such as Cl• and •CH₃ are neutral; the dot shows an unpaired electron, not a charge. Cl⁻ is charged but has all its electrons paired, so it is not a radical.

This is an older meaning of 'radical', as in the 'sulfate radical' of older textbooks. In IB chemistry a radical is a species with an unpaired electron: Cl• is a single atom yet is a radical, and SO₄²⁻ is not a radical.
An incomplete octet is not the test. BF₃ and CH₃⁺ have only six electrons around the central atom but all are paired, so they are not radicals. What matters is an unpaired electron.
questions.explain: This is the definition: a radical has an unpaired electron, as in •CH₃ and Cl•. The unpaired electron is what makes radicals highly reactive.

questions.q: Methane reacts with bromine in ultraviolet (UV) light. Which equation represents the initiation step?
options: Br₂ → Br⁺ + Br⁻
CH₄ → •CH₃ + H•
Br₂ → Br• + Br•
CH₄ → CH₃⁻ + H⁺
optionWhy: This is heterolytic fission, with one atom taking both electrons. The initiation step is homolytic: each Br atom takes one electron, giving two neutral radicals and no ions.
The C–H bond in methane is much stronger than the Br–Br bond, so UV light breaks Br–Br, not C–H. The C–H bond is broken later, in propagation, by a Br• radical, and no H• is formed.

UV light supplies the energy to break the Br–Br bond homolytically: one electron of the bonding pair goes to each atom, giving two bromine radicals. The Br–Br bond is much weaker than a C–H bond, so it is the bond that breaks.
Methane does not ionize: carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativities, so the C–H bond is essentially non-polar. The initiation step is the homolytic fission of the much weaker Br–Br bond.
questions.explain: UV light supplies the energy to break the Br–Br bond homolytically: one electron of the bonding pair goes to each atom, giving two bromine radicals. The Br–Br bond is much weaker than a C–H bond, so it is the bond that breaks.

questions.q: In the homolytic fission of Cl₂, two single-barbed (fish-hook) arrows are drawn, each starting at the Cl–Cl bond and ending at a different chlorine atom. What does each arrow represent?
options: The movement of an electron pair
The movement of a chlorine atom
The release of stored bond energy
The movement of one electron
optionWhy: A pair is shown by a double-barbed curly arrow. If each of the two arrows moved a pair, four electrons would leave a bond that holds only two.
Mechanism arrows show electrons, not atoms. The atoms separate because the electrons move; each arrow tracks one electron.
Arrows do not show energy, and no energy stored in the bond is released: breaking the Cl–Cl bond absorbs energy (242 kJ mol⁻¹, supplied by UV light or heat).
A single barb means one electron. Each arrow moves one electron of the Cl–Cl bonding pair to a different chlorine atom, so each atom becomes Cl•.
questions.explain: A single barb means one electron. Each arrow moves one electron of the Cl–Cl bonding pair to a different chlorine atom, so each atom becomes Cl•.

questions.q: Cyclohexane reacts with chlorine in UV light. Which equation represents a propagation step of this reaction?
options: C₆H₁₂ + Cl• → C₆H₁₁Cl + H•
•C₆H₁₁ + Cl₂ → C₆H₁₁Cl + Cl•
•C₆H₁₁ + Cl• → C₆H₁₁Cl
C₆H₁₂ + Cl⁺ → C₆H₁₁Cl + H⁺
optionWhy: Cl• does not swap directly for a hydrogen atom. It removes a hydrogen atom to form HCl, leaving a cyclohexyl radical: C₆H₁₂ + Cl• → •C₆H₁₁ + HCl. No H• radical forms.

A propagation step has one radical on each side: •C₆H₁₁ reacts with a Cl₂ molecule to form chlorocyclohexane and a new Cl• radical, which carries the chain on. The other propagation step is C₆H₁₂ + Cl• → •C₆H₁₁ + HCl.

Two radicals combining is a termination step, not propagation: radicals are removed and none is formed. It does make some chlorocyclohexane, but most forms in propagation, •C₆H₁₁ + Cl₂ → C₆H₁₁Cl + Cl•.
This step uses ions, but radical substitution involves no ions. Initiation is homolytic fission, which gives Cl• radicals rather than Cl⁺, and each propagation step has one radical on each side.
questions.explain: A propagation step has one radical on each side: •C₆H₁₁ reacts with a Cl₂ molecule to form chlorocyclohexane and a new Cl• radical, which carries the chain on. The other propagation step is C₆H₁₂ + Cl• → •C₆H₁₁ + HCl.

questions.q: The products of the reaction of methane with chlorine in UV light include CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄. How are most of these more highly substituted products formed?
options: Cl• removes an H atom from a chloromethane; the radical then reacts with Cl₂
Cl• replaces an H atom in a chloromethane directly, releasing a free H• radical
Chlorinated methyl radicals combine with Cl• in termination, the main source of products
Each forms in one step, e.g. CH₃Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + HCl, as its equation shows
optionWhy: Cl• attacks C–H bonds in chloromethanes as it does in methane, e.g. CH₃Cl + Cl• → •CH₂Cl + HCl, then •CH₂Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + Cl•. Repeating these propagation steps gives CHCl₃ and CCl₄.
Cl• does not swap for H. It removes a hydrogen atom as HCl, leaving a radical such as •CH₂Cl, which then takes a Cl atom from Cl₂. No H• radical is formed.
Radical–radical combinations are rare because radicals are present at very low concentration. Termination makes a little of these products, but most form in propagation steps with Cl₂.

An overall equation is the sum of mechanism steps, not a single collision. Each further substitution happens by the same radical propagation steps: Cl• removes an H atom, then the radical reacts with Cl₂.
questions.explain: Cl• attacks C–H bonds in chloromethanes as it does in methane, e.g. CH₃Cl + Cl• → •CH₂Cl + HCl, then •CH₂Cl + Cl₂ → CH₂Cl₂ + Cl•. Repeating these propagation steps gives CHCl₃ and CCl₄.

questions.q: Alkanes react with very few reagents. Which statement explains the low reactivity of alkanes?
options: Their C–C and C–H bonds are strong and are essentially non-polar.
They are saturated, and saturated compounds are unreactive.
Each atom has a full outer shell, so the molecule is unreactive.
Strong intermolecular forces hold the molecules together.
optionWhy: Strong bonds need a large energy input to break, and because carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativities the bonds have no significant partial charges for polar reagents to attack.
Many saturated compounds react readily: halogenoalkanes and alcohols are saturated. Saturation rules out addition, but alkanes' low reactivity is due to their strong, essentially non-polar bonds.
Full outer shells are found in nearly every stable molecule, including reactive ones such as CH₃Cl and HCl. Reactivity depends on bond strength and polarity, not on full shells.
Reactions break covalent bonds within molecules, not forces between them. In any case the forces between alkane molecules are weak London forces; methane boils at −162 °C.
questions.explain: Strong bonds need a large energy input to break, and because carbon and hydrogen have similar electronegativities the bonds have no significant partial charges for polar reagents to attack.

questions.q: Which statement describes how a nucleophile forms a new bond to its reaction partner?
options: It donates both electrons of the new covalent bond.
It accepts the two electrons of the new covalent bond.
It gives one electron, and its partner gives the other.
It transfers electrons, forming an ionic bond.
optionWhy: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor: it supplies both electrons of the new bond, usually from a lone pair, and the electrophile supplies none.
Accepting the pair is what an electrophile does. 'Nucleophile' means nucleus-seeking: it is the electron-rich partner and donates the pair.
That is how a covalent bond is pictured in dot-and-cross diagrams such as H₂, but in a nucleophile–electrophile reaction the nucleophile supplies both electrons of the new bond.
'Donate' here means supply for sharing. The pair ends up shared between the two atoms, so the new bond is covalent (e.g. the C–O bond in an alcohol), not ionic.
questions.explain: A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor: it supplies both electrons of the new bond, usually from a lone pair, and the electrophile supplies none.

questions.q: 1-bromopropane is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide. Which equation represents the reaction that occurs?
options: CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂⁻ + HOBr
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Br⁻
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CHBr⁻ + H₂O
CH₃CH₂CH₂Br + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH⁻ + Br
optionWhy: This has OH⁻ bonding to the bromine atom. Br is the δ− end of the C–Br bond; an electron-rich nucleophile is attracted to the δ+ carbon, so the C–O bond forms and Br⁻ leaves.
OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon bonded to Br, and the C–Br bonding pair leaves with Br as the bromide ion. The product is propan-1-ol.
This treats OH⁻ as a base removing H⁺ from carbon. With a halogenoalkane, OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile: it donates its lone pair to the carbon bonded to Br, substituting for the halogen.

This splits the C–Br bonding pair one electron to each atom, so Br leaves as an atom. In substitution the C–Br bond breaks heterolytically: Br takes both electrons and leaves as Br⁻, and the alcohol is neutral.
questions.explain: OH⁻ donates a lone pair to the δ+ carbon bonded to Br, and the C–Br bonding pair leaves with Br as the bromide ion. The product is propan-1-ol.

questions.q: Which statement describes the heterolytic fission of a covalent bond?
options: One bonding electron goes to each fragment, so radicals form.
Both bonding electrons go to one fragment, so two ions form.
Both bonding electrons go to one fragment, which becomes positive.
It is the breaking of a bond that joins two different elements.
optionWhy: An even split of the bonding pair is homolytic fission, which gives radicals. Heterolytic fission gives both electrons to one fragment, forming ions.
In heterolytic fission one fragment keeps the bonding pair and becomes an anion; the other becomes a cation, e.g. H–Br → H⁺ + Br⁻.
A fragment that takes both electrons gains negative charge, so it becomes the anion. The fragment left without the pair becomes the cation.

'Hetero-' describes the two different fragments formed (a cation and an anion), not the atoms in the bond. A bond between different atoms can break either way: C–Cl breaks heterolytically when a nucleophile substitutes for Cl, but homolytically in UV light, giving radicals.
questions.explain: In heterolytic fission one fragment keeps the bonding pair and becomes an anion; the other becomes a cation, e.g. H–Br → H⁺ + Br⁻.

questions.q: Hydrogen chloride undergoes heterolytic fission to form H⁺ and Cl⁻. Which describes the curly arrow for this change?
options: It starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on the H atom.
It starts on the Cl atom and points back to the H–Cl bond.
It starts on the H atom and shows the H⁺ ion moving away.
It starts at the H–Cl bond and ends on the Cl atom.
optionWhy: If the pair went to H, H would become H⁻ and Cl would become Cl⁺. The product H⁺ shows that H has lost its share of the pair, so the arrow ends on Cl.
An arrow starting on Cl and ending on the bond would show electrons moving INTO the bond, which forms a bond rather than breaking one. Start at the source of the pair: the H–Cl bond.
A curly arrow never shows an atom or ion moving; it shows an electron pair. The pair in the H–Cl bond moves to Cl, and H⁺ is what is left behind.
A curly arrow shows an electron pair moving from its source to its destination. The H–Cl bonding pair moves onto Cl, which becomes Cl⁻, leaving H⁺.
questions.explain: A curly arrow shows an electron pair moving from its source to its destination. The H–Cl bonding pair moves onto Cl, which becomes Cl⁻, leaving H⁺.

questions.q:
Ethene reacts with bromine:
CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br
Which reactant acts as the electrophile?
options: Br₂, as it accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond
Ethene, as its C=C bond is rich in electrons
Neither, as neither reactant carries a positive charge
Ethene, as its C atoms need electrons for an octet
optionWhy: Br₂ accepts the electron pair donated by the electron-rich C=C bond, forming a C–Br bond. A neutral molecule can be an electrophile.
It is true that the C=C bond is electron-rich, but that makes ethene the electron-pair DONOR, the nucleophile. The electrophile is the electron-pair acceptor, Br₂.
An electrophile need not be charged. Br₂ accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond, so it is the electrophile, even though it is neutral.
Each carbon in C=C already has an octet. The C=C bond is electron-rich and donates a pair; Br₂ accepts it, so Br₂ is the electrophile.
questions.explain: Br₂ accepts the electron pair donated by the electron-rich C=C bond, forming a C–Br bond. A neutral molecule can be an electrophile.

questions.q: Why are alkenes susceptible to attack by electrophiles?
options: The C=C double bond is weaker than a C–C single bond.
The C=C double bond is a region of high electron density.
The carbon atoms of C=C are deficient in electrons.
The C=C carbon atoms need more electrons for an octet.
optionWhy: C=C is stronger than C–C (it has a higher bond enthalpy). Alkenes react because of the high electron density of the double bond, not because it is weak.
The double bond concentrates electron density between and around the two carbon atoms, and this electron-rich region attracts electron-pair acceptors.
An electrophile seeks electrons, so it attacks an electron-RICH site. The carbon atoms of C=C are surrounded by high electron density, not a deficit.
Each carbon in C=C shares four electron pairs and already has an octet. The reason is the high electron density of the double bond.
questions.explain: The double bond concentrates electron density between and around the two carbon atoms, and this electron-rich region attracts electron-pair acceptors.

questions.q: Ethene is bubbled through a solution of bromine in an organic solvent at room temperature, in the dark. Which statement is correct?
options: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂BrCH₂Br forms by addition.
The bromine loses its colour as CH₂=CHBr forms by substitution.
No reaction occurs, as Br₂ has no positive charge.
No reaction occurs, as UV light is needed to split Br₂.
optionWhy: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.
Replacing an H atom and keeping C=C is how alkanes react (with UV light). Alkenes react by addition, and the product 1,2-dibromoethane has no C=C bond.
An electrophile need not be positive. Neutral Br₂ accepts an electron pair from the C=C bond, so the reaction occurs and the colour disappears.
UV light is needed for radical substitution of alkanes. Alkenes react with Br₂ rapidly in the dark, which is why bromine is used to test for C=C.
questions.explain: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.
